why: This chapter is a chain of worked problems: urns, witnesses who lie or err, and the fractions that follow. Prose cannot show whether the fractions are right, so the lens leads with recomputable calculations, one per problem, with the witness's reliability on a slider. The argument that connects the problems, and the people Laplace uses as warnings, get a short tree and a cast list.

lenses.title: Number 79 from an urn of a thousand
lenses.why: Laplace states each step as a printed fraction, so every step can be recomputed and compared.

src.q: A single number has been drawn from an urn which contains a thousand of them. A witness to this drawing announces that number 79 is drawn; one asks the probability of drawing this number.
experience has made known that this witness deceives one time in ten
an urn which contains a thousand of them

steps.label: Probability that his testimony is true

src.q: so that the probability of his testimony is 1/10

steps.note: The premise says he deceives one time in ten, so his testimony is true 9 times in 10. The transcriber's note promises two corrections on page 110, '9/10 in place of 1/10' and '9/10 in place of 6/10'; this file contains neither.

erratum.q: Two further corrections have also been made: 9/10 in place of 1/10, and 9/10 in place of 6/10, on page 110

steps.label: He tells the truth: 79 is drawn and he says so

src.q: the probability that the witness will announce number 79 is the probability itself of the drawing of this number, that is to say, 1/1000. It is necessary to multiply it by the probability 6/10 of the veracity of the witness; one will have then 9/10000 for the probability of the event observed in this hypothesis.

steps.note: With the veracity of 9/10 that the premise implies, the printed result is right: the operand, not the product, is the misprint.

erratum.q: Two further corrections have also been made: 9/10 in place of 1/10, and 9/10 in place of 6/10, on page 110

steps.label: He deceives: 79 was not drawn

src.q: If the witness deceives, number 79 is not drawn, and the probability of this case is 999/1000.

steps.label: …and of the 999 numbers not drawn he names 79

src.q: the probability that he will choose number 79 is 1/999; multiplying, then, this probability by the preceding one, we shall have 1/1000 for the probability that the witness will announce number 79 in the second hypothesis.

steps.label: …times the chance that he deceives

src.q: It is necessary again to multiply this probability by 1/10 of the hypothesis itself, which gives 1/10000 for the probability of the event relative to this hypothesis.

steps.label: Probability that 79 was drawn (the sixth principle)

src.q: the probability of the first hypothesis, and this probability will be 9/10; that is to say, the veracity itself of the witness.

steps.note: For any size of urn the answer equals the witness's veracity: with numbered balls a liar has 999 lies to choose from, so his lie rarely lands on 79.

plot.caption: P(79 drawn) against veracity: the diagonal. Testimony to one number out of many is worth exactly the witness's veracity.

lenses.title: One white ball among 999 black: the extraordinary fact
lenses.why: The chapter's central result. A liar who sees black has only one false thing to say, so his lies all land on 'white'.

src.q: Suppose now that the urn contains 999 black balls and one white ball, and that one ball having been drawn a witness of the drawing announces that this ball is white.

lenses.title: The argument of the chapter
lenses.why: Between the calculations Laplace argues a single thesis against named opponents.

nodes.text: The more extraordinary the fact attested, the more probable it is that the witness errs or lies.

src.q: Applying this conclusion to all extraordinary deeds it results from it that the probability of the error or of the falsehood of the witness becomes as much greater as the fact attested is more extraordinary.

children.text: The white-ball urn: a single liar's falsehood has only one place to land.

src.q: We see thus how the probability of the falsehood increases in the measure that the deed becomes more extraordinary.

children.text: Allowing the witness to be honestly mistaken, as well as to lie, makes the extraordinary still less credible.

src.q: We have supposed up to this time that the witness was not mistaken at all; but if one admits, however, the chance of his error the extraordinary incident becomes more improbable.

children.text: Some authors: seeing an extraordinary fact is like seeing an ordinary one, so the witness deserves equal credence.

src.q: Some authors have advanced the contrary on this basis that the view of an extraordinary fact being perfectly similar to that of an ordinary fact the same motives ought to lead us to give the witness the same credence when he affirms the one or the other of these facts.

children.text: Common sense rejects this, and the calculus measures how far.

src.q: Simple common sense rejects such a strange assertion; but the calculus of probabilities, while confirming the findings of common sense, appreciates the greatest improbability of testimonies in regard to extraordinary facts.

children.text: Two equally credible witnesses: one saw a man dead fifteen days ago, the other saw him alive yesterday. Each fact alone is ordinary.

src.q: These authors insist and suppose two witnesses equally worthy of belief, of whom the first attests that he saw an individual dead fifteen days ago whom the second witness affirms to have seen yesterday full of life.

children.text: An impossible conclusion is the limit of extraordinary ones; urns A and B show how far combined testimony loses value.

src.q: but an impossible conclusion is the limit of extraordinary conclusions, as error is the limit of improbable conclusions

children.text: So a suspension of natural laws needs an immense weight of testimony; ordinary rules of criticism do not apply.

src.q: One may judge by this the immense weight of testimonies necessary to admit a suspension of natural laws, and how improper it would be to apply to this case the ordinary rules of criticism.

children.text: Dominant opinion can make the absurd look credible: Racine and Pascal on a Port-Royal miracle.

src.q: Two great men of the century of Louis XIV.—Racine and Pascal—are striking examples of this.

children.text: Pascal's wager, in Craig's geometric form, fails: the infinite promise itself makes the testimony infinitely improbable.

src.q: Also calculus teaches us that this exaggeration itself enfeebles the probability of their testimony to the point of rendering it infinitely small or zero.

children.text: Independent witnesses who agree are more credible the less probable the fact is in itself.

src.q: One sees by this how much the probability of the falsehood of the witnesses diminishes when the fact which they attest is less probable in itself.

children.text: Testimony passed down a chain of witnesses decays; time erodes historical facts as it erodes monuments.

src.q: The action of time enfeebles then, without ceasing, the probability of historical facts just as it changes the most durable monuments.

children.text: Craig computed when the proofs of Christianity would fade out; Laplace calls the analysis faulty.

src.q: he finds that this ought to take place 1454 years after the time when he writes. But his analysis is as faulty as his hypothesis upon the duration of the moon is bizarre.

lenses.title: Where Laplace limits his own rule
lenses.why: The chapter's strongest rule has an exception that Laplace states himself.

cases.rule: Testimony to an extremely improbable event deserves no credence.

ruleSrc.q: We would give no credence to the testimony of a man who should attest to us that in throwing a hundred dice into the air they had all fallen on the same face.

cases.case: Had we seen it ourselves and checked for illusion and deception, we would accept it. Improbability alone is not impossibility.

src.q: But after this examination we should not hesitate to admit it in spite of its extreme improbability; and no one would be tempted, in order to explain it, to recur to a denial of the laws of vision.

cases.note: Venn takes up this same example in his footnote 7 (chapter XVII).

xref.label: Venn, ch. XVII, n. 7
xref.q: Laplace, for instance (_Essai_, ed. 1825, p. 149), says that if we saw 100 dies

cases.rule: Reports of events contrary to natural law lower belief in what they report.

ruleSrc.q: All those who without offering this immensity of testimonies support this when making recitals of events contrary to those laws, decrease rather than augment the belief which they wish to inspire

cases.case: Among the uneducated the wonderful raises belief instead: what lowers credence for some raises it for others.

src.q: But that which diminishes the belief of educated men increases often that of the uneducated, always greedy for the wonderful.
